The lesson puts scoping in Detection & analysis, which comes before containment, so a learner could argue for scoping first via the SIEM and then isolating everything at once (E then B). Also, once B cuts the network, E's 'live connections' are really connection state left in memory, not active links; worth rewording. E is also much longer and more specific than the other steps, but length doesn't give away its position. Not a blocker.

Statement 7 ('Record how long detection took') contains the word 'detection', which pulls a learner toward Detection & analysis. isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.answer: The four phases are preparation, detection and analysis, containment/eradication/recovery, and post-incident activity. You contain first to stop the attack spreading and to cut off the attacker's control. Eradicating before you have contained it risks the attacker re-infecting systems or moving elsewhere while you clean. You keep a compromised machine powered on because memory holds running processes and live network connections, and that volatile evidence is lost at shutdown. A playbook is the written plan for one specific type of incident, such as ransomware or a compromised mailbox, set out as concrete steps with named owners. The post-incident lessons-learned review feeds back into preparation, so the plan and playbooks get better before the next incident.
isc2.cc.d2.incident-response::isc2.cc.d2.note: The prompt asks 'why you contain before you eradicate', but the lesson's own reason is weak: it only says containment stops spreading, and it gives the reason for eradicating before recovery instead. A scorer's rubric should accept 'stops spread/attacker control while you clean'.

The other half of the statement (one failure each across 300 accounts over an afternoon) already identifies spraying, so drop 'all with the same password' or reword it as an inference.
